name: Chandpur
tagline: The hilsa capital of Bangladesh — where the Padma, Meghna and Dakatia meet at the Molhead, the country's biggest ilish market runs at dawn, and the river launches from Dhaka dock all day.

guide.bestTime: July to October for the hilsa season and a full, broad river; October to February for cool weather, the mosques and the riverfront. Note the roughly 22-day hilsa ban in October, when the fish goes off-market.
guide.gettingThere: The classic way is the Dhaka–Chandpur launch down the Meghna (one of the country's busiest routes); also by train via Laksam (the Sagarika / Meghna Express) or by road from Comilla and Chittagong. The Molhead and fish market are in Chandpur town; Hajiganj and Shahrasti lie east on the Comilla road.
guide.difficulty: Easy — the town sights cluster around the riverfront, and the launch trip is half the fun. The confluence current is genuinely strong; stay behind the railings at the Molhead.

mustVisit.name: Tin Nodir Mohona (Boro Station Molhead)
mustVisit.description: The 'meeting of three rivers' — Padma, Meghna and Dakatia — at the tip of Chandpur town, where a long concrete promenade juts into the water past the Rakta Dhara monument. The district's signature view and its favourite sunset gathering.
mustVisit.history: The Molhead embankment was built to protect the town and its railway/launch station from erosion at this volatile confluence; the Rakta Dhara memorial honours the area's 1971 martyrs.

howToReach.fromDistrictTown: In Chandpur town, walkable from the launch terminal, Chandpur Sadar
howToReach.transport: Rickshaw / on foot from the launch ghat

mustVisit.bestTime: Late afternoon for sunset; Oct–Mar for calmer water
tips: The current at the point is strong — stay behind the railings, don't wade
Combine with the adjacent Boro Station hilsa market in the morning

mustVisit.name: Hajiganj Boro Masjid
mustVisit.description: One of the largest mosques in the subcontinent by capacity — about 28,400 sq ft, holding some 10,000 worshippers — with a soaring ~188-ft minaret and marble-and-stone domes. A major Friday and Eid congregation site.
mustVisit.history: The site began as a prayer house after the Sufi Mokimuddin settled here; the masonry mosque's foundation was laid around 1930 by Maulana Abul Farah Jainpuri, with the first azan a few years later.

howToReach.fromDistrictTown: About 25 km east of town on the Chandpur–Comilla road, Hajiganj Upazila

mustVisit.bestTime: Cool months; avoid prayer times for a quiet visit
tips: Modest dress required; non-Muslims should ask before entering the prayer hall
Near Hajiganj railway station — easy to reach by train

mustVisit.name: Hazrat Shah Rasti (RA) Mazar
mustVisit.description: The tomb-shrine of the 14th-century Sufi saint who gives Shahrasti upazila its name, set beside a large historic dighi with a three-domed mosque. A pilgrimage and ziyarat site, busiest at the annual urs.
mustVisit.history: Shah Rasti, said to have reached Bengal around 1351 among the companions of Shah Jalal, died around 1388; the shrine was raised over his tomb three centuries later on the order of Pari Bibi, daughter of Mughal subedar Shaista Khan.

howToReach.fromDistrictTown: About 35–40 km east/southeast at Sreepur, Shahrasti Upazila

mustVisit.bestTime: The urs (last Thursday of Magh, Jan–Feb); otherwise cool mornings
tips: Shoes off at the shrine; expect crowds during the urs
Women should check access at the inner tomb

mustVisit.name: Angikar Sculpture
mustVisit.description: Chandpur town's principal 1971 memorial — a roughly 15-ft figural sculpture of freedom fighters set beside a lake in the town centre, and a civic gathering point.
mustVisit.history: Installed in 1989 and created by sculptor Syed Abdullah Khalid — the artist behind Dhaka's Aparajeyo Bangla — to commemorate the district's liberation struggle.
tips: An easy stroll from the Molhead
Pair with a riverfront walk at dusk

mustVisit.name: Rupsa Zamindar Bari
mustVisit.description: A roughly 250-year-old zamindar estate in Faridganj with old residential buildings and grounds — a window into the district's landed-gentry past.
mustVisit.history: Founded after the earlier Hindu zamindars declined, when a Muslim landlord bought the zamindari from the British; the Rupsa landlords are locally remembered as benevolent.

howToReach.fromDistrictTown: About 30 km south of town at Rupsa, Faridganj Upazila

tips: Parts are old and decayed — watch your footing

mustVisit.name: Boro Station Hilsa Market
mustVisit.description: The country's biggest hilsa wholesale and landing market, on the riverfront beside the Molhead — a dawn spectacle of boats, ice and silver ilish auctioned by the maund.
mustVisit.history: The market grew around Chandpur's role as the natural collection point for hilsa from the Padma–Meghna and the southern coast; it remains the reference point for national hilsa prices.

practical.hours: Early morning; peak in the Jul–Oct season

howToReach.fromDistrictTown: At the Molhead / Boro Station, Chandpur Sadar
howToReach.transport: Rickshaw / on foot from the launch ghat

mustVisit.bestTime: Sunrise, July to October (closed during the October ban)
tips: Go at sunrise for the auctions
Catching and selling hilsa is banned during the ~22-day October breeding ban — plan around it

specialties.name: Padma-Meghna Hilsa (Ilish)
specialties.description: Chandpur's ilish is regarded as the freshest and finest in the country. Eaten as shorshe ilish (mustard), ilish bhaja (fried), or panta-ilish with fermented rice — the monsoon and Pohela Boishakh ritual.
specialties.venue: Boro Station fish market & town restaurants (Jul–Oct)

specialties.name: River-Fish Bhorta
specialties.description: Mashed and curried freshwater fish with mustard oil, onion and chilli — the staple riverine plate across the district.

specialties.name: Pitha & Mishti Doi
specialties.description: Winter rice cakes (pitha) and sweet curd and sweetmeats from the town's confectioners — the everyday Bengali sweet tradition.

bucketlist.title: Watch three rivers meet at the Molhead
bucketlist.detail: The Padma, Meghna and Dakatia converge at the tip of Chandpur town — a long promenade into the water, busiest and most beautiful at sunset.

bucketlist.title: Watch the dawn hilsa auction at Boro Station
bucketlist.detail: The country's biggest ilish market — boats, ice and silver fish auctioned by the maund as the sun comes up.

bucketlist.title: Take the Dhaka–Chandpur launch
bucketlist.detail: One of the busiest river routes in the country — a few hours down the Meghna from Sadarghat, the classic way to arrive.

bucketlist.title: Eat shorshe ilish at the source
bucketlist.detail: Hilsa in mustard gravy, cooked from fish landed that morning — nowhere fresher than Chandpur.

bucketlist.title: Stand under the Hajiganj Boro Masjid minaret
bucketlist.detail: A mosque holding 10,000 worshippers, its ~188-ft minaret among the tallest in the region.

bucketlist.title: Visit the Shah Rasti shrine and dighi
bucketlist.detail: The 14th-century Sufi saint who named Shahrasti, his tomb beside a great tank and three-domed mosque.

bucketlist.title: See the Angikar sculpture
bucketlist.detail: Chandpur's 1971 memorial by Syed Abdullah Khalid — freedom fighters in bronze beside a town-centre lake.

bucketlist.title: Try panta-ilish on Pohela Boishakh
bucketlist.detail: Fermented rice with fried hilsa — the Bengali New Year plate, eaten with green chilli and onion.

bucketlist.title: Wander the Rupsa Zamindar Bari
bucketlist.detail: A ~250-year-old zamindar estate in Faridganj, its old buildings slowly returning to green.

bucketlist.title: Walk the Dakatia riverbank
bucketlist.detail: The Dakatia loops through the district before joining the Meghna at the Molhead — quiet ghats and fishing boats.

bucketlist.title: Drift the confluence by boat
bucketlist.detail: Hire a small boat off the Molhead at dusk to feel the scale of three great rivers meeting.

bucketlist.title: Buy sweet curd from a town confectioner
bucketlist.detail: Chandpur's old sweet shops turn out mishti doi and pitha to round off a river meal.

foods.name: Padma-Meghna Hilsa (Ilish)
foods.description: Regarded as the freshest, finest hilsa in the country — shorshe ilish, ilish bhaja, or panta-ilish, from fish landed that morning.
foods.whereToFind: Boro Station fish market & town restaurants (Jul–Oct)

foods.name: River-Fish Bhorta
foods.description: Mashed, curried freshwater fish with mustard oil, onion and chilli, eaten with rice — staple riverine fare.

foods.name: Panta-Ilish
foods.description: Fermented rice with fried hilsa, green chilli and onion — the Pohela Boishakh and monsoon ritual plate.

foods.name: Mishti Doi & Pitha
foods.description: Sweet curd and winter rice cakes from the town's confectioners — the everyday Bengali sweet.

famousPeople.name: Shankha Ghosh
famousPeople.knownFor: Major Bengali poet and literary critic, winner of the Jnanpith Award (2016) and many of Bengal's highest literary honours. Born in Chandpur in 1932 (with ancestral roots in Banaripara, Barisal).

famousPeople.name: Monirul Islam
famousPeople.knownFor: Internationally renowned printmaker and etcher, recipient of the Ekushey Padak (1999) and Spanish royal honours, who divides his life between Dhaka and Madrid. Born in Chandpur in 1943.

famousPeople.name: Dildar
famousPeople.knownFor: One of Bangladesh's most beloved film comedians, a fixture of Dhallywood cinema for decades. From Chandpur district.

didYouKnow: Chandpur is the 'hilsa (ilish) capital of Bangladesh' — its Boro Station is the country's largest hilsa landing and wholesale market.
The town sits at the confluence of three rivers — Padma, Meghna and Dakatia — the famous Tin Nodir Mohona at the Molhead.
The district's name is traced either to the zamindar Chand Rai or to the Sufi Chand Faqir — two competing folk etymologies.
Shahrasti upazila is named after the Sufi saint Hazrat Shah Rasti, who died there around 1388.
Hajiganj Boro Masjid is among the largest mosques in the subcontinent by capacity, holding around 10,000 worshippers under a ~188-ft minaret.
Chandpur became a subdivision in 1878 but a full district only in 1984, split from greater Comilla — despite its town being a busy river port since the 19th century.
